words: Stenger argues that pervasive misery fits an evil deity better than a good one, challenging divine-grounding accounts to reconcile objective morality with suffering.
critique: Strongest feature: Stenger directly contrasts pervasive worldly misery with divine goodness, arguing that observed suffering fits an evil deity better, which makes the objection especially responsive and logically intelligible. Principal limitation: The excerpt offers no substantiation beyond suffering’s asserted prevalence, and evil-deity compatibility neither demonstrates inconsistency between misery and unidentified divine intentions nor addresses morality’s claimed objective, nonintersubjective divine grounding. Live burden: Stenger must connect suffering specifically to the morality arguments by establishing that their divine foundation entails benevolence and cannot accommodate apparently gratuitous misery. Locked score: The exact score of 66 fits because responsiveness and relevance are comparatively strong through direct contact, whereas evidence warrant and calibration toward possible divine intentions remain materially weaker.
